executiveSummary: OpenAI said its models proved the Exponential Time Hypothesis false and found new math and physics results, and outside experts are now organizing independent review.
Community researchers spent all week reading and steering single neurons in Qwen, moving from a 'humble muffin' to a full database of every neuron in two models.
Anthropic filed to go public with a startling insurance risk factor, Binance reportedly lost $5.6B to hackers, and Patrick Stewart died at 86.

stories.title: OpenAI claims its models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis and found new Kakeya and QCD results; roon: 'and then losing'
stories.overview: OpenAI announced three AI-produced discoveries: a local smoothing result tied to the Kakeya conjecture, a Lean-verified refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and results on the existence of QCD. Complexity theorists were asked to run an open review of the ETH claim. Reactions ranged from awe to calls that the result was 'somewhat deflationary,' and @tszzl used the announcement to predict how humans would lose control of an intelligence explosion. These are claims still under verification, but they were the week's biggest AI science story.
stories.connection: @tszzl's 'bits and atoms' post directly quoted @danintheory's announcement of OpenAI's three discoveries, and the next day's discussion folded in Axiom's own Lean formalization milestone.
stories.continuityNote: Two weeks ago the fight was over OpenAI's flood of AI math manuscripts; this week OpenAI claimed a headline refutation of a major complexity conjecture and handed it to outside experts to check.

continuesFrom.title: "They have annihilated my field of research" / "CLAUDE FOUND THE SEEDS": AI math results from OpenAI and Anthropic

dailyStories.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false.
wow I didn't know you could DO that with mere bits and atoms

segments.commentary: The announcement came from OpenAI's own leadership and researchers, framed as three discoveries in three fields.
The ETH claim drew the most attention, and @AndrewCurran_'s blunt one-liner became the meme version of the news.
What gave the claim weight was @rrwilliams saying he, Impagliazzo and Paturi would organize an open, independent examination.
The next day @tszzl read it as a preview of losing control, while Axiom showed formal verification scaling to a 15,000-page proof.

tweets.name: Dan Roberts
tweets.text:
The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem.

Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean.

The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.

Our system found its natural language disproof for the ETH we reached out to to @rrwilliams. Ryan will form a collaboration with Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi to verify and shepherd this result. Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and Williams has refuted strong versions of the ETH, used ETH for hardness results, and connected algorithms and lower bounds.

This group asked us to make all raw data of the results public to facilitate independent verification by the community, which we have done by posting the natural language proof and Lean formalization to our GitHub repo. The group also invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.

https://t.co/fkLJX9a2Zi

stories.title: From a green neuron to a 'humble muffin' to Neuron Lens: the week the community read Qwen's neurons
stories.overview: A playful find by @Sauers_ of a neuron that 'makes the model green' set off a week of single-neuron experiments on Qwen. @jfonsecarivera published a searchable library of 34,220 persona neurons, others shared steering recipes for an 'evil qwen,' and @maxsloef trained a whole persona into one neuron. @voooooogel warned that steering-induced persona shifts may be 'persona solving' rather than proof of persona neurons. By Saturday @_a9lim and @treetowntree had released Neuron Lens, a database of every neuron and attention head in two models.
stories.connection: All five daily stories are the same community thread on reading and steering individual neurons, mostly in Qwen: josh credited @Sauers_ for his library, J-lens was pitched as the next step, the owl and persona-solving posts responded to the 'persona neurons' trend, and Neuron Lens is the full release of J-lens.

dailyStories.title: I found a neuron that makes the model green.
i made a library of 34,220 persona neurons in qwen
turns out it's possible to read neurons directly, via J-lens!
You can turn Qwen3-8B into an owl by training only one random neuron!
neuron lens: a database of every single neuron and attention head in qwen 3 8b and gemma 4 12b

segments.commentary: It started half as a joke, and replies treated it as pure mechinterp delight.
Two days later @jfonsecarivera turned the idea into a toy everyone could play with, swept with Haiku and rated by weirdness.
The play quickly got a darker edge, with a reproducible recipe for steering one neuron to make the model evil.
@_a9lim previewed a way to read what neurons mean instead of guessing from steering.
Friday brought both an escalation and a caution: one trained neuron can make an owl, but steering results may not mean a neuron is persona-specific.
The week ended with the full release, which its authors say predicts steering results over 90% of the time.

tweets.name: a9lim
tweets.text:
@treetowntree and i created neuron lens: a database of every single neuron and attention head in qwen 3 8b and gemma 4 12b read using the R-lens (a J-lens variant) and what we call the "S-lens". you can find it at https://t.co/DI2Cpajc3M, along with the tools we used to make it. 

using the R-lens to read neurons' input and output projections turns out to be very effective at determining what a neuron does. we're able to legibly read what a majority of neurons do when fired: the lens qualitatively predicts the result of steering over 90% of the time!

the same trick lets us read attention heads' QK circuits and OV circuits, showing us both what they attend to and what they do with it. however, the R-lens has two important flaws: its accuracy degrades in early layers, and it can't separate the MLP block and the attention block.

we found ways around both these issues. we first modified the r-lens by fitting it on input tokens rather than output tokens to get the s-lens, which is accurate in early layers but inaccurate in late layers. we then fitted R- and S-lenses to the activations after attention but before the MLP to get "mid-lenses", which are much better at deciphering MLP inputs and attention outputs. using both of these techniques, we were able to interpret most of the models' layers.

stories.title: Anthropic files its S-1, says no insurer could cover its risk, and staff start counting their millions
stories.overview: Anthropic filed for its IPO, and the community zeroed in on a risk factor saying the whole insurance industry could not cover the catastrophic risk the company poses. Posters also passed around reported first-half revenue of $16.3 billion. Two days later the filing fed back-of-envelope math that about 1 in 70 Americans worth $100M+ would be Anthropic staff, alongside a viral post about technical workers feeling their skills are useless.
stories.connection: @jakehalloran1's wealth estimate and the follow-up share-price math were built on Anthropic's S-1 filing from two days earlier.

dailyStories.title: Anthropic has filed an S-1 registration statement with the SEC related to its proposed IPO.

segments.commentary: The filing itself was a short legal notice, but it was the most-liked post of its day.
The insurance language became the instant talking point, read as either alarming or classic histrionic risk-factor boilerplate.
Others went straight to the revenue numbers in the filing.
By Thursday the talk had turned to what the IPO means for lab employees' wealth, and to unease among everyone else.

tweets.name: Colossus
tweets.text:
The people of Silicon Valley are unwell.

If you work at a frontier lab or decacorn, you’ve got it bad. You haven’t seen your kids, your girlfriend’s annoyed, invites from friends to hang out are waning, even weddings are on hold. This is the time to make your mark and make your money, after all.

If you’re building a startup that’s trying to compete with or be one of these companies, you’ve got it bad. Maybe you passed up a job offer at one a couple years back, which means you left $100M on the table, you fucking idiot. Being an underdog isn't as fun as you thought.

If you’re working on a pre-AI startup, you’ve got it bad. Not too long ago you were the belle of the ball, but now your 30% year-on-year growth doesn’t feel like growth at all. It feels like death.

"Too many of my friends are spiraling," Brie Wolfson writes. "I don’t know how we’re supposed to live and work like this."

It’s all too much, too fast. Too much money, too much growth, too much power, too much change. Every month, a new frontier model is released. Every day, a new unicorn is minted. Seriously. 300 days into the year 2026, and 311 unicorns have been minted so far.

So what’s left for the sane ones? Brie went looking for teams playing a different game. She found one in Ottawa: a search infrastructure company that many of the AI darlings rely on.

It's growing fast, and its people are well.

Read @zebriez’s latest company dispatch from inside the sane asylum of turbopuffer.

https://t.co/wn0zpo9Gld

stories.title: Patrick Stewart, Captain Picard, has died at 86
stories.overview: Patrick Stewart's death was announced from his own account, which asked for donations to Alzheimer's research and caregiver support in place of flowers. Community members went beyond routine tributes, describing Picard as a moral ideal and a model of empathetic masculinity, and remembering his years of Shakespeare and stage work.

stories.title: Binance reportedly hacked for $5.6B as Polymarket halts trading and an open model exploits Firefox
stories.overview: A breaking post claimed Binance lost over $5.6 billion, which would make it the largest hack in crypto history. The same day Polymarket halted trading after a third-party provider was compromised, and Epoch AI showed the open-weight GLM 5.3 reliably building Firefox exploits from published but unshipped fixes for about $1,000 per version. patio11 summed up the mood: attackers used to be 'rate-limited on cognition.' The Binance figures were reported, not confirmed.

dailyStories.title: Binance hacked with over $5.6 billion stolen

segments.commentary: The headline number came from an aggregator's breaking post, with a coin-by-coin breakdown.
Polymarket's halt hours earlier made it feel like a wave rather than a single incident.
Epoch's experiment explained why people were nervous: cheap AI can now turn public patches into working exploits.

tweets.name: Epoch AI
tweets.text:
In recent experiments, we found that GLM 5.3 can autonomously compromise recent versions of Mozilla Firefox using security fixes that have been published but not yet shipped to users.

We used a deliberately basic setup meant to emulate a relatively unsophisticated attacker with limited resources. After basic initial instructions to inspect those not-yet-shipped fixes, the model reliably built successful exploits for six recent Firefox versions on its own using only information available at the time of release.

These exploits, which cost about $1,000 per compromised version, would let an attacker steal passwords and authentication cookies stored in the browser, or read any files on the user's computer, after the user opens a single webpage, with no further interaction.

The exploits make use of the "patch gap," the time between when security fixes are made public in beta or "nightly" software updates and when those fixes are generally released to users. Until now, exploiting it required significant human time and skill, or special access to frontier models with advanced cyber capabilities.

Our results show that widely available open-weight models can now do this relatively cheaply and quickly. We gave GLM 5.3 up to 48 hours to find an exploit, but its fastest attempt needed only 12 hours.

In all of its successful attacks, the patch gap gave GLM 5.3 an initial foothold in the browser. To turn that foothold into reading files off the user's computer, the model also independently discovered and used a previously unpublished vulnerability.

We shared our findings with Mozilla, which patched the vulnerability in its October 27 Firefox 159.0 release. We haven't yet confirmed whether the attack still succeeds without it, but expect the fix makes it substantially harder. We're grateful to Mozilla for their responsiveness and collaboration.
